title: Phased capacity-aware deployment playbook (working)
summary: Working notes + checklist for rolling out features with explicit awareness of GPU capacity, queue/backpressure behavior, and cost impacts. Focus: small-batch exposure tied to capacity signals, automated throttles and staged increase heuristics for LLM deployments.
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures a practical, cross-functional approach for phased rollouts that explicitly considers model serving capacity and backpressure characteristics. It complements canary & A/B experiment guidance by making capacity the dominant signal for exposure decisions rather than purely user-signal heuristics.

Audience:
- Product managers owning exposure strategy
- SRE / Infra engineers who operate GPU pools
- Serving runtime / platform engineers who implement throttles, batching, and fallbacks
- Oncall / incident responders

Why this is different:
Many rollout playbooks assume traffic slices are safe if user metrics look stable. For LLMs, a small traffic increase can cause outsized queueing or token-cost spikes. This playbook treats capacity as a first-class gating dimension and provides operational recipes to escalate exposure only as serving capacity proves stable.

High-level approach (phases):
1) Internal dogfood + synthetic load (0% user traffic)
   - Run feature behind a flag in staging and in a mirrored prod path with synthetic requests that mimic expected prompt length and concurrency.
   - Validate latency, queue depth, effective batch sizes, token cost per request.
2) Micro-exposure (0.1% - 0.5%)
   - Route tiny slice of real user traffic for real-signal validation.
   - Strict capacity gates enforced (see gating signals).
3) Capacity-stepped growth (0.5% -> 5% -> 20%)
   - Increase allocation only when capacity signals are green and cost-latency curves remain within budget.
4) Region/Pool expansion
   - After single-pool validation, expand to additional pools/regions using same checks.
5) Full activation with ongoing autoscaling rules

Key signals (primary, must be observed at each step):
- GPU queue depth (requests waiting in serving queue) — threshold: < 10 for stable, 10-50 caution, >50 require rollback or throttle
- 95th and 99th latency for token-stream completion — compare to baseline; >25% increase triggers pause
- Token/sec throughput per GPU (utilization) — ensure not exceeding tested plateaus; sustained >90% util is a red flag for thin margin
- Batch sizes distribution — sudden shift to much larger batch sizes can change tail latency; prefer stable distribution matching synthetic profile
- Cost per 1k tokens (runbook-calculated) — sudden >15% increase vs baseline needs investigation
- Model fallback error rate (e.g., fallbacks to smaller models) — must be <1% long-term during growth steps

Automated gating rules (implementation suggestions):
- A deployment automation job evaluates the signals in 10-minute windows. To advance one step, require 3 consecutive windows that pass all thresholds.
- If any primary signal crosses red threshold for 2 consecutive windows, automatically reduce traffic to previous safe level and page oncall.
- Soft-warning tier (yellow) for single-window blips: alert to Slack #deployments but do not auto-roll back.

Example phased allocation schedule (template):
- Week 0: Internal synthetic test (0%) — 24–48h run
- Day 1: Micro-exposure 0.1% for 4 hours — gating check
- Day 1-2: If green, 0.5% for 12 hours
- Day 3: If green, 1–2% for 24h
- Day 4: If green, 5% for 48h
- Day 7: If green, 20% for 72h then ramp to 50%/100% as capacity allows
Notes: timings are heuristics; replace with faster or slower cadence depending on user risk and usage patterns.

Traffic shaping and fallback behaviors:
- Prefer deterministic partitioning (hashed by user-id) so cohorts are stable and avoid thundering herd when rollback occurs.
- Implement immediate per-cohort throttle cap: if cohort's requests/sec > expected by X% (configurable), route to baseline model.
- Fallback cascade: feature-variant -> smaller model variant -> baseline model -> 503 with maintenance header. Each step records metrics for postmortem.

Operational checklist (pre-rollout):
- [ ] Confirm baseline performance profile for target model(s) using representative prompts (store artifacts in Confluence link above).
- [ ] Run synthetic load jobs that mimic 99th-percentile concurrency and prompt lengths.
- [ ] Provision a dedicated canary pool (or tag subset of GPUs) and confirm isolation.
- [ ] Add capacity-aware alarms to PagerDuty routing (queue depth + token cost alarms).
- [ ] Confirm rollback playbooks and who owns each step (PM, SRE, runtime eng).
- [ ] Schedule oncall coverage during rollout windows and pre-alert stakeholders.

Quick runbook for oncall (if alarms fire):
1) Check gates dashboard (latency, queue depth, per-pool utilization)
2) If queue depth > 50: reduce traffic to prior step immediately and confirm cascading fallback is active
3) If 95/99 latency > threshold: check batch size distribution and KV-cache hit rate; if unfamiliar, page runtime owner
4) If token-cost spike: disable caching bypasses and consider temporary model quantization fallback if available
5) Create incident channel and capture timeline and last config changes; do not expand exposure until fixed.

Data and dashboards we need (minimal):
- Real-time cohort-level view: exposure fraction, users impacted, per-request median/95/99 latencies, token cost, fallback rate
- Pool-level hardware telemetry: GPU util, memory pressure, queue depth, recent SKUs used
- A/B comparison slices: user impact on engagement and quality metrics over time windows

Housekeeping for experiments and audits:
- Persist a rollout manifest per feature: model version, pool ids, exposure fractions over time, config hashes. This is required for postmortem cost accounting.
- Tag all GitHub PRs and deploys with rollout-id so telemetry links back to code changes.

Open questions and tradeoffs to resolve (action items):
- How conservative should default thresholds be for the micro-exposure step? (proposal: start conservative, then move to calibrated defaults per product line)
- Do we require dedicated canary pools for all paid customers? (tradeoff: cost vs isolation)
- Should we automate cohort shrinking if utilization rises, or do manual steps? (proposal: automation for severe signals, manual for borderline)

Proposed next steps (short term):
- PM & SRE: finalize threshold table for Queue/Latency/TokenCost by 2025-03-07 (owner: Aisha).
- Runtime: implement 3-window gating check in rollout automation and add ability to step traffic down programmatically (owner: Samir).
- Console: add single-pane cohort telemetry with fast-action buttons to reduce/increase slices and trigger fallback cascade (owner: Lena).

Notes to reviewers:
This is intended to be a working operations playbook that you can implement incrementally. Feedback wanted on the gating windows, default numeric thresholds, and whether the exposure cadence should be calendar-based or signal-only.

Appendix: quick numeric thresholds (initial defaults)
- Pass condition per 10-minute window: queue_depth_95 < 20, latency_95 < 1.25x baseline, gpu_util_95 < 90%, batch_size_shift < 10%
- Yellow: queue_depth_95 between 20-50 OR latency_95 between 1.25x-1.5x baseline OR gpu_util_95 between 90-95%
- Red: queue_depth_95 > 50 OR latency_99 > 1.5x baseline OR sustained gpu_util_95 > 95%

Unresolved:
- How to reconcile cost spikes when traffic appears evenly distributed? Need deeper tooling to attribute token-cost anomalies to prompt distribution changes vs model behavior.

End of doc.
